mcqs.question: Why is L1 cache almost always split into separate instruction and data caches, while L2/L3 are usually unified?
options: Because instructions and data use physically different voltage levels
Because splitting lets instruction fetch and data access happen without contending for the same ports, which matters most at L1's tight per-cycle timing
Because unified caches can't be made small enough for L1's size budget
Because the ISA requires separate address spaces for code and data
mcqs.explanation: L1 splits I-cache/D-cache mainly for port contention and timing reasons — the CPU fetches an instruction and accesses data in the same cycle, and separate small caches avoid a structural conflict at that tight latency budget. It's not about voltage, cache size limits, or ISA address-space rules.

mcqs.question: Why is L3 typically shared across all cores rather than private to each core like L1?
options: Sharing lets L3 flexibly serve whichever core needs capacity most, and gives cores a fast common point to see data another core recently touched
Private L3 caches are technically impossible to build
Sharing L3 eliminates the need for any cache coherence protocol
L3 is shared purely to reduce total chip cost, with no performance benefit
mcqs.explanation: A shared L3 avoids duplicating hot data per core and gives a fast common meeting point for inter-core data sharing — a genuine performance benefit, not just a cost save. It doesn't eliminate coherence protocols; if anything, L3 is often deeply involved in coherence tracking. Private L3 designs do exist in some systems, so it isn't technically impossible.

mcqs.question: What is the main trade-off an inclusive multi-level cache accepts, and what does it gain in return?
options: It wastes outer-level capacity duplicating inner-level lines, in exchange for a simple, fast way to check whether any core holds a given line
It uses more power per access, in exchange for a faster clock speed
It requires more comparator hardware per set, in exchange for a higher hit rate
It loses the ability to hold instructions, in exchange for holding more data
mcqs.explanation: Inclusion means every L1 line is duplicated in L2/L3, wasting some outer-level capacity — but it lets a coherence check consult just the outer level to know whether any core might have the line cached, rather than having to probe every core's private caches. Power, clock speed, comparator count, and instruction/data split are unrelated to the inclusion decision.
